A recent report from Counterpoint Research points out that, with pricing pressure from rising memory costs, the US entry-level smartphone market in Q2 2026 is under strain, with smaller manufacturers being hit particularly hard, as larger brands are better positioned to absorb rising component costs. Details as follows.

Rising memory costs hit budget smartphones hardest

According to Counterpoint Research, combined US smartphone sales of Apple, Samsung, Motorola and Google in Q2 2026 fell 4% year-on-year, while sales for the rest of the market plunged 45% — all because smaller manufacturers struggled to cope with rising component costs.

Counterpoint notes that smartphone sales under US$100 in Q2 2026 dropped nearly 65% from a year earlier, which反而 boosted Samsung's and Motorola's market share in the prepaid segment, as rising component costs narrowed the price gap between their entry-level models and white-label smartphones.

Turning to Apple, the report notes that while the company has kept iPhone pricing unchanged in the US market, it has simultaneously raised prices on other products. Counterpoint expects the company to "raise prices on iPhone 18 series models," with some models expected to be unveiled in a few weeks.

Below is the full report:

Analyst Jeff Pu forecast just last week that the iPhone 18 Pro would be priced in the US$1,349 to US$1,399 range, the iPhone 18 Pro Max at US$1,449 to US$1,499, while multiple reports also point to the iPhone Ultra starting at around US$2,500.

Apple reported its Q3 2026 results late last month, with iPhone revenue up 22% year-on-year to US$54.2 billion. The company also cautioned the market that memory costs and supply constraints would worsen significantly in the September quarter, with a particularly pronounced impact on iPhone, iPad and Mac.
